description: The 6Cs -- six practitioner qualities that turn person-centred values into day-to-day care.
content_html:
What Are the 6Cs?

The 6Cs are six qualities every health and social care practitioner needs to do their job well. They were originally introduced into NHS nursing practice in 2012 as part of a drive to improve standards following high-profile failures in care, and they have since become widely adopted as a framework for what good practice looks like at the individual practitioner level. They sit under section 2.1 of the specification as a separate bullet from the nine person-centred values — they are the practitioner’s own characteristics, not the principles of what good care looks like for the service user.

Think of person-centred values as the destination and the 6Cs as the engine. A practitioner who lacks compassion cannot deliver the value of dignity; a practitioner who lacks courage cannot uphold a service user’s rights when doing so is difficult. The 6Cs answer the question: what kind of person do you need to be to deliver person-centred care?

Key Fact

The 6Cs are: Care, Compassion, Competence, Communication, Courage and Commitment. They are qualities of a service practitioner, not principles of care delivery. They are tested separately from the nine person-centred values and should never be written as if they are the same thing.

Care

Care is the central quality — it is the reason health and social care exists as a profession. A practitioner who demonstrates care notices when something is wrong even when the service user has not said anything, goes beyond the minimum required by their role and treats the service user’s wellbeing as the priority. At Sunrise Nursing Home, an HCA who spots that a resident has barely touched her meals for two days and raises it with the charge nurse is demonstrating the quality of care: she is actively promoting wellbeing rather than waiting to be told there is a problem.

Compassion

Compassion is the quality that brings emotional warmth to the practitioner’s technical skills. A community nurse visiting a 68-year-old man with a newly diagnosed chronic condition applies compassion by listening fully before explaining the diagnosis, acknowledging how frightening the news might feel and checking that the service user feels supported before ending the visit. Compassion enables the value of dignity: a service user who feels the practitioner genuinely cares about their experience is less likely to feel humiliated or treated as a task to be completed.

Competence

Competence means having the skills and knowledge to do the job correctly. A pharmacy technician applying competence dispenses the right medication at the right dose and checks for contraindications before handing it to the patient. Competence is not just technical — it also means knowing when you are outside your competence and need to refer to a colleague or supervisor. A key worker who does not have the training to assess a safeguarding risk and therefore escalates to the Designated Safeguarding Lead is demonstrating competence, not weakness.

Communication

The quality of communication in the 6Cs means more than simply talking to service users. It includes listening actively, choosing appropriate language (no jargon), adjusting tone and pace for different service users and communicating effectively with colleagues across a multi-professional team. A receptionist at a GP surgery who explains a wait time clearly, uses a calm tone and asks if the patient needs to sit near the entrance applies good communication as a quality. A ward nurse who handovers patient information accurately to the night team also demonstrates this quality — poor communication between professionals is one of the most common causes of errors in care settings.

Courage

Courage is the quality that enables practitioners to act when acting is hard. It might mean challenging a colleague who is cutting corners, raising a safeguarding concern even when you are not certain, or telling a service user a difficult truth rather than avoiding the conversation. A healthcare assistant who witnesses a colleague handling a service user roughly and reports it to a senior member of staff is demonstrating courage. Without this quality, poor practice goes unchallenged and service users suffer. Courage is closely linked to the value of rights: upholding a service user’s right to protection from abuse and harm sometimes requires a practitioner to take uncomfortable action.

Commitment

Commitment means being reliably dedicated to the service user’s wellbeing over time. A support worker who attends training on new moving and handling techniques, keeps up to date with changes in guidance and consistently applies person-centred values throughout their career — not just in their first week — demonstrates commitment. This quality also extends to the organisation: commitment means advocating for improvements in the care setting, not just doing the minimum required each shift.

Key Fact

Each of the 6Cs links to one or more person-centred values: Care → individuality, rights; Compassion → dignity, respect; Competence → rights, protection; Communication → choice, encouraging decision making; Courage → rights, protection; Commitment → all values sustained over time. An exam answer that names a 6C AND explains which value it enables will score higher than one that defines the 6C alone.

Yemi is a nurse at a busy NHS walk-in centre. Her next patient is Tomasz, a 34-year-old man from Poland who has a painful leg wound and limited English. Yemi demonstrates all six qualities during the consultation. She actively examines the wound thoroughly (competence). She speaks slowly, uses simple language and fetches a bilingual information card (communication). She notices Tomasz looks frightened and reassures him with a calm, warm manner (compassion). She cleans and dresses the wound carefully, monitoring his pain levels throughout (care). She documents the case accurately and flags it for follow-up (commitment). When she notices a safeguarding concern suggested by the pattern of the injury, she reports it to the charge nurse despite being uncertain (courage). The 6Cs work together, not in isolation.

A very common error in exam answers about Topic Area 2 is to write “the nine person-centred values include compassion and competence” or to list a 6C as if it were a value. The nine values are: individuality, choice, rights, independence, privacy, dignity, respect, partnership and encouraging decision making. The 6Cs are: Care, Compassion, Competence, Communication, Courage and Commitment. They are different lists. If a question asks you to “describe how a practitioner can deliver person-centred values”, you should name the values and explain the practitioner behaviours. The 6Cs can be referenced as the qualities that enable the practitioner to deliver those values, but naming a 6C as a value will lose marks. Keep the lists separate in your revision.
exam_tip_html: For a 6-mark extended-response question on the 6Cs, the most common error is to define each quality briefly rather than developing two or three of them with a reasoning chain. The command word ‘Explain’ requires “reasons for and/or causes of” — use ‘because’, ‘therefore’ and ‘this means that’ in every paragraph. A strong answer names the quality, explains what the practitioner does as a result of possessing it, links it to a specific person-centred value it enables, and applies it to the named setting and service user in the question. For example: “Yemi demonstrates compassion by acknowledging Tomasz’s fear before explaining the treatment plan, therefore Tomasz feels respected and his dignity is upheld, this means that he is more likely to engage honestly with the care he receives.” Two or three developed points like this will score higher than six brief definitions.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The 6Cs (Care, Compassion, Competence, Communication, Courage, Commitment) are the six personal qualities of a service practitioner that enable them to deliver person-centred values effectively.
  • The 6Cs are NOT the same as the nine person-centred values — they are listed as a separate bullet in the specification and tested separately. Never list a 6C as a value or vice versa.
  • In exam answers, link each 6C to the person-centred value it enables and apply it to the named setting and service user — this is what earns the application and analysis marks.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is one of the 6Cs?
A) Individuality
B) Compassion
C) Partnership
D) Dignity
practice_questions.marks: B) Compassion [1 mark]. (Individuality, Partnership and Dignity are person-centred values, not 6Cs.)

1 mark for correctly naming two of the 6Cs: Care, Compassion, Competence, Communication, Courage, Commitment. Both must be from this list. Do not accept person-centred values such as dignity or respect.

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by the quality of competence in a health or social care practitioner.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the core meaning (having the knowledge, skills and ability to carry out professional duties safely and to the required standard); 1 mark for a qualifying detail (e.g. knowing when you are outside your competence and need to refer to a colleague or supervisor; having up-to-date training to perform tasks correctly).

practice_questions.text: Describe how a healthcare assistant on a hospital ward could demonstrate two of the 6Cs when supporting an elderly service user.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks per 6C. Example: Compassion (2 marks) -- 1 mark for naming the quality; 1 mark for a specific ward action and its effect (e.g. sitting at the service user's eye level and speaking gently when explaining their medication options, so that the service user feels understood and respected). Care (2 marks) -- 1 mark for naming the quality; 1 mark for a specific action (e.g. checking the service user's fluid intake and nutrition without being asked, noticing any deterioration and reporting it to the nurse in charge, so that the service user's physical wellbeing is actively promoted). Other 6Cs accepted with relevant ward examples.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the quality of courage is important for a practitioner working in a residential care home.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying the quality of courage and what it involves (willingness to challenge poor practice, speak up or report a concern); 1 mark for a reason using 'because' (e.g. because care homes support vulnerable older adults who may not be able to report poor practice themselves); 1 mark for a developed consequence (e.g. therefore without courage, poor practice goes unchallenged and service users' right to protection from abuse and harm is not upheld).

practice_questions.text:
Priya is a key worker at Sunfield Community Centre, which runs a daily drop-in service for adults experiencing homelessness. One of the service users, 41-year-old Marcus, has a history of mental health difficulties and has not engaged with any support service for several months. He has just walked in for the first time.

Explain how Priya could use the 6Cs when supporting Marcus during his first visit. In your answer, refer to specific qualities and link them to the person-centred values they enable.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Names at least three 6Cs clearly, explains what Priya does as a result of each quality in the context of Marcus's specific circumstances (homelessness, mental health difficulties, first visit, community centre setting). Links each 6C to a person-centred value it enables. Uses reasoning chains with 'because', 'therefore' or 'this means that'. Example content: Compassion -- Priya listens without interrupting and acknowledges how difficult things have been for Marcus, therefore he feels understood and his dignity is upheld, this means that he is more likely to engage with the support available. Communication -- Priya speaks calmly and uses straightforward language, avoiding clinical jargon, because Marcus may feel anxious and overwhelmed, so this means he can take in the information and feel reassured. Courage -- If Marcus mentions something concerning about his safety, Priya documents and reports it to her line manager even if she is not certain, because his right to protection from harm is her duty to uphold. Commitment -- Priya follows up on his next visit and ensures his support plan is reviewed, because consistent support is particularly important for someone who has disengaged in the past.

Secure (3-4 marks): Identifies at least two 6Cs with mostly accurate explanation and some application to Marcus's situation.

Developing (2 marks): Names qualities but explanation is descriptive; limited application to Marcus.

Emerging (1 mark): Names one quality with little or no explanation.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is one of the 6Cs of a service practitioner?
Which statement best describes the relationship between the 6Cs and person-centred values?
options: The 6Cs are the practitioner's qualities that enable them to deliver person-centred values
The 6Cs and person-centred values are different names for the same list
The 6Cs are the values that service users are entitled to
The 6Cs replace person-centred values in larger care settings

knowledge_checks.q: The 6C of _____ means having the knowledge, skills and ability to carry out professional duties safely.
The 6C of _____ means speaking up, challenging poor practice and doing what is right even when it is difficult.

right: Sensitivity to distress with warmth and empathy, enabling dignity and respect
Long-term dedication to improving care and developing professional skills
Exchanging information clearly and sensitively, adapted to the service user's needs

flashcard_questions.a: Six qualities of a service practitioner: Care, Compassion, Competence, Communication, Courage and Commitment.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Care mean as one of the 6Cs?
flashcard_questions.a: Actively promoting and maintaining the physical, emotional, social and intellectual wellbeing of service users.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Compassion mean as one of the 6Cs?
flashcard_questions.a: Sensitivity to the distress of others, delivered with warmth, empathy and genuine concern.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Competence mean as one of the 6Cs?
flashcard_questions.a: Having the knowledge, skills and ability to carry out professional duties safely and to the required standard.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Communication mean as one of the 6Cs?
flashcard_questions.a: Exchanging information clearly and sensitively, adapted to the needs of the service user and situation.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Courage mean as one of the 6Cs?
flashcard_questions.a: The willingness to speak up, challenge poor practice and act in the service user's best interests even when difficult.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Commitment mean as one of the 6Cs?
flashcard_questions.a: Long-term dedication to improving care, developing professional skills and maintaining the highest standards.

flashcard_questions.q: Which person-centred value does Compassion most directly enable?
Which person-centred value does Courage most directly enable?
flashcard_questions.a: Rights and protection from abuse and harm.

flashcard_questions.q: Are the 6Cs the same as the nine person-centred values?
flashcard_questions.a: No. Person-centred values are principles of care for the service user; the 6Cs are qualities the practitioner must possess.

flashcard_questions.q: What 6C does a practitioner demonstrate by reporting a safeguarding concern even when uncertain?
flashcard_questions.a: Courage -- the willingness to act in the service user's best interests even when it is uncomfortable.

glossary_terms.definition: Six qualities of a health and social care practitioner (Care, Compassion, Competence, Communication, Courage, Commitment) that enable the delivery of person-centred values.
Actively promoting and maintaining the physical, emotional, social and intellectual wellbeing of service users as the core purpose of the practitioner's role.
Sensitivity to the distress of others and the desire to help alleviate it, delivered with warmth, empathy and genuine concern.
Having the knowledge, skills and ability to carry out professional duties safely and to the required standard, including knowing when to refer.
The willingness to speak up, challenge poor practice, advocate for service users and do what is right even when it is difficult or uncomfortable.
A long-term dedication to improving care, developing professional skills and maintaining the highest standards for service users over time.
